easy.prompt: In the relational model, what is a relation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A foreign-key link between two tables.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A query that joins multiple tables.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A table — a set of tuples (rows) sharing the same attributes (columns).

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single row identified by a primary key.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A relation is the mathematical name for a table: a set of rows with a fixed schema.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes a referential constraint, not a relation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A join is an operation over relations, not the relation itself.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A row is a tuple; the whole table is the relation.

easy.prompt: What is the purpose of a primary key?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To uniquely identify each row in a table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To link a child row to a parent row in another table.

choices.label: C
choices.body: To speed up every SELECT query automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To store the largest value in each column.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: A primary key guarantees entity integrity: no two rows share the same key value.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is the role of a foreign key.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Indexes may help lookups, but that is not the definition of a primary key.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Keys identify rows; they are not aggregate summaries.

easy.prompt: A foreign key enforces what kind of integrity?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Referential integrity between child and parent rows.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Domain integrity on numeric columns only.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transactional durability after COMMIT.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Entity integrity within a single table.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Foreign keys require that referenced parent values exist (or use defined ON DELETE/UPDATE actions).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Domain constraints apply to data types and allowed values, not cross-table links.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Durability is an ACID property, not referential integrity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Entity integrity is enforced by the primary key.

easy.prompt: In an ER diagram, a one-to-many relationship between Department and Employee means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Each employee belongs to at most one department; a department can have many employees.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Departments and employees must share the same primary key.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Each employee can belong to many departments simultaneously in this relationship.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Each department has exactly one employee.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: One-to-many is the usual works-for pattern: many employees, one department per assignment.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Related tables use separate keys linked by foreign keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes many-to-many.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That would be one-to-one, not one-to-many.

easy.prompt: Which SQL clause filters rows before they are grouped?

choices.label: A
choices.body: ORDER BY

choices.label: B
choices.body: GROUP BY

choices.label: C
choices.body: WHERE

choices.label: D
choices.body: HAVING

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: ORDER BY sorts the final result set.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: GROUP BY forms groups; it does not filter row-level predicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: HAVING applies predicates to grouped results, not to raw rows.

easy.prompt: What does SELECT DISTINCT do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Sorts rows in ascending order.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Locks the table for exclusive write access.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Returns only the first row of the table.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Removes duplicate rows from the query result.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: DISTINCT applies to the full projected row: identical combinations appear once.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Use ORDER BY to sort.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Locking is a transaction concern, not DISTINCT.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Use LIMIT 1 for a single row; DISTINCT removes duplicates, not all but one.

easy.prompt: Which statement adds a new row to an existing table?

choices.label: A
choices.body: INSERT

choices.label: B
choices.body: CREATE TABLE

choices.label: C
choices.body: ALTER TABLE

choices.label: D
choices.body: UPDATE

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: INSERT supplies values for a new tuple; UPDATE modifies existing rows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: CREATE TABLE defines a new relation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ALTER changes schema (columns, constraints), not row data.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: UPDATE changes existing rows.

easy.prompt: DELETE removes rows; what does DROP TABLE do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Removes only rows that fail a WHERE clause but keeps the table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rolls back the last transaction.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Removes the table definition and all its data from the schema.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Renames the table while preserving all rows.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: DROP is DDL that destroys the relation; DELETE is DML that removes selected rows.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes DELETE with a predicate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Use ROLLBACK to undo a transaction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Use RENAME/ALTER RENAME for renaming.

easy.prompt: First normal form (1NF) requires that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every determinant is a candidate key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Each cell holds a single atomic (indivisible) value and repeating groups are eliminated.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All joins are lossless without projection.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: 1NF bans nested lists and multi-valued cells in a single column.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That characterizes BCNF, not 1NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is 3NF-style dependency rules.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Lossless join is a decomposition property, not 1NF.

easy.prompt: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every table has exactly one column.

choices.label: B
choices.body: No non-key attribute depends on a proper subset of a composite primary key.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All foreign keys reference surrogate keys only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every index is clustered on the primary key.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: 2NF removes partial dependencies: attributes must depend on the whole key, not part of it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 2NF allows composite keys; it concerns partial dependencies.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Surrogate keys are a design choice, not part of 2NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Indexing is physical design, not normal form.

easy.prompt: Why are indexes created on database columns?

choices.label: A
choices.body: To replace the need for a primary key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: To speed up data retrieval at the cost of extra storage and write overhead.

choices.label: C
choices.body: To guarantee that every query returns sorted results.

choices.label: D
choices.body: To enforce that no two transactions run concurrently.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Indexes are auxiliary access paths (often B-trees) that reduce scan cost for selective lookups.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Primary keys enforce uniqueness; indexes are optional helpers.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: ORDER BY controls sort order; indexes only help if the planner uses them.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Concurrency is controlled by locking and isolation, not indexes.

easy.prompt: A typical B-tree index supports which operation efficiently?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Arbitrary Cartesian products without sorting.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Point lookups and range scans on the indexed key order.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Full table scans faster than reading heap pages.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Guaranteed O(1) lookup regardless of table size.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: B-trees keep keys sorted in balanced pages, enabling log-time seeks and ordered range reads.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Join algorithms still matter; indexes do not eliminate join cost.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Sequential heap scans often beat random index probes for low selectivity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: B-tree height grows with table size (logarithmic, not constant).

easy.prompt: What is a database transaction?

choices.label: A
choices.body: A network connection between client and server.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Any SELECT statement that returns more than one row.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A sequence of operations executed as a single logical unit of work.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A permanent schema change applied with ALTER TABLE.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Transactions group reads and writes so they commit or roll back together.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A session/connection can host many transactions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A multi-row SELECT is not necessarily transactional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: DDL may be transactional in some systems but is not the definition.

easy.prompt: Atomicity in ACID means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every query runs in constant time.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The database schema never changes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Concurrent transactions never block each other.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Either all operations in a transaction take effect, or none do.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Atomicity is all-or-nothing: partial updates are rolled back on failure.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Complexity is unrelated to atomicity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Schema can change; atomicity applies to a transaction's effects.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would ignore locking; isolation handles concurrency.

easy.prompt: Consistency in ACID means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: No transaction may ever abort.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All replicas return identical answers at every instant.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A committed transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, honoring constraints.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Indexes are always kept in memory.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Consistency is about invariant rules (keys, checks, triggers) holding after commit.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Transactions may abort to preserve consistency.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a distributed replication concern, not the ACID definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Storage layout is implementation detail.

easy.prompt: Isolation in ACID means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Every table has at most one row.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Backups run only on weekends.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Concurrent transactions behave as if they did not interleave in problematic ways.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Data is encrypted on disk.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Isolation levels define which interleavings are visible (dirty reads, phantoms, etc.).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Tables can have many rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Backup scheduling is operational, not ACID isolation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Encryption is security, not isolation.

easy.prompt: Durability in ACID means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Queries never use the write-ahead log.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Uncommitted changes are visible to all users.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Indexes are rebuilt on every SELECT.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Committed changes survive crashes and restarts.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Once COMMIT succeeds, the system must recover committed data after failure (often via WAL).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: WAL is a common durability mechanism.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would violate isolation, not define durability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SELECT should not rebuild indexes.

easy.prompt: What does COMMIT do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Makes a transaction's changes permanent and visible to other sessions (per isolation rules).

choices.label: B
choices.body: Creates a new index on every column.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Deletes the database file.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Undoes all changes made since the transaction began.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: COMMIT ends the transaction successfully; ROLLBACK discards changes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Indexes are created explicitly with DDL.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: COMMIT persists work; it does not drop the database.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is ROLLBACK.

easy.prompt: What does ROLLBACK do?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Increases the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE automatically.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Permanently saves changes to disk.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exports the entire schema to CSV.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Discards uncommitted changes made in the current transaction.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: ROLLBACK aborts the transaction and restores the pre-transaction view for that session.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Isolation is set explicitly, not by ROLLBACK.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is COMMIT.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Export tools are separate from transaction control.

easy.prompt: A surrogate key is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: An artificial identifier (e.g., auto-increment ID) with no business meaning.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A foreign key pointing to two parent tables at once.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A checksum of all non-key columns.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A natural key derived from government-issued numbers only.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Surrogate keys stabilize joins when natural keys are composite or change over time.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: A foreign key references one parent relation (possibly composite).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Checksums detect corruption; they are not primary keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Natural keys come from the domain (email, ISBN), not surrogates.

medium.prompt: An INNER JOIN between Orders and Customers returns…

choices.label: A
choices.body: All orders plus customers with NULLs where no match exists.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All customers even if they placed no orders.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only rows with matching keys in both tables.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The Cartesian product of every order with every customer.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps matches on the join predicate; non-matching rows are dropped.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That describes a LEFT OUTER JOIN from orders.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is RIGHT/LEFT OUTER from the customer side.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CROSS JOIN omits an equality predicate; INNER JOIN requires one.

medium.prompt: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?

choices.label: A
choices.body: LIMIT

choices.label: B
choices.body: SELECT DISTINCT

choices.label: C
choices.body: HAVING

choices.label: D
choices.body: WHERE

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: HAVING predicates apply to grouped aggregates (e.g., COUNT(*) > 10).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: LIMIT caps row count after the query is evaluated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: WHERE filters rows before grouping.

medium.prompt: A LEFT OUTER JOIN from A to B keeps…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only rows from B when A has no match.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Rows from A only if B has at least two matching rows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only rows that match in both A and B.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All rows from A, with NULLs in B's columns when no B row matches.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: LEFT OUTER preserves the left side entirely and pads missing right-side values with NULL.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That would be RIGHT OUTER from B's perspective.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Joins do not require multiple matches on the right.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is an INNER JOIN.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Transitive dependencies: non-key attributes depending on other non-key attributes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Repeating groups within a single cell.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Multivalued dependencies between independent facts.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key only.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: 3NF requires non-key attributes depend only on keys, not on other non-key attributes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is addressed by 1NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is 4NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is 2NF.

choices.label: A
choices.body: All attributes are multi-valued.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Foreign keys may not exist.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every table has no more than three columns.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every determinant of a functional dependency is a candidate key.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: BCNF strengthens 3NF: if X → Y, then X must be a superkey.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: BCNF assumes relational values (1NF).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: BCNF allows foreign keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: BCNF is about dependencies, not column count.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reduce join cost and speed read-heavy workloads at the expense of update anomalies.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Eliminate the need for indexes entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Guarantee BCNF in every table automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Prevent any redundant data from ever existing.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Denormalization trades redundancy for performance in OLAP or hot read paths.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Indexes remain useful on denormalized tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Denormalization intentionally introduces redundancy.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Denormalization adds redundant copies.

medium.prompt: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) helps most when a query…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Filters only on first_name with no predicate on last_name.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Selects all rows with SELECT * without a WHERE clause.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Updates unrelated columns in random order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Filters or sorts on last_name, or on both columns in that order.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Composite B-tree indexes support left-prefix matching: leading column must be constrained for efficiency.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Skipping the leading column often prevents index use.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Full scans ignore selective index benefit.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Write patterns affect maintenance cost but not this lookup rule.

medium.prompt: A covering index for a query is one that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stores only NULL values for faster scans.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Includes all columns needed by the query so the engine can satisfy it from the index alone.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replaces the primary key constraint.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Spans every table in the database schema.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Index-only scans avoid heap lookups when projected columns are in the index payload.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: NULL handling exists but covering means included columns, not NULL-only.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Covering indexes complement, not replace, keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Indexes are per-table (or per-partition) structures.

choices.label: A
choices.body: An index is missing on a foreign key.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two or more transactions wait on each other's locks in a cycle.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A single transaction runs longer than one second.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The database runs out of disk space during SELECT.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Circular wait-for graphs cause deadlock; engines abort one victim transaction.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Missing indexes hurt performance but do not define deadlock.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Long transactions are problematic but not deadlock by definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is resource exhaustion, not lock cycling.

medium.prompt: A lost update anomaly happens when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The database loses power before COMMIT.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A transaction reads uncommitted data from another session.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A transaction sees new rows inserted by another transaction on re-read.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Two transactions read the same value, compute new values independently, and the later write overwrites the earlier without merging.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Lost update is a write-write conflict without proper locking or versioning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That concerns durability, not lost updates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is a dirty read.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is a phantom read.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Reading the same row twice with identical results under repeatable read.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reading data written by another transaction that has not yet committed.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Reading only committed data at snapshot time.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Reading an empty table after TRUNCATE in another session that rolled back.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Dirty reads see uncommitted changes that may be rolled back.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Repeatable read prevents non-repeatable reads, not dirty reads by definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That is consistent snapshot behavior.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: If the other transaction rolled back, you should not see TRUNCATE effects—dirty read is about uncommitted writes.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Dirty reads.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deadlocks entirely.

choices.label: C
choices.body: All write skew anomalies without extra locking.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All phantom reads in every database engine.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: READ COMMITTED hides uncommitted data; phantoms and write skew may still occur.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Deadlocks can occur at any isolation level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Write skew needs careful constraints or SERIALIZABLE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Phantom prevention usually needs higher isolation or locking.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Rows read earlier in the transaction appear unchanged on subsequent reads in the same transaction.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All sessions see identical global snapshots forever.

choices.label: C
choices.body: No new rows can ever be inserted into the database.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every SELECT uses a full table lock on all tables.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Repeatable read stabilizes existing rows; phantoms may still appear depending on engine.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Snapshots are per-transaction, not permanent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inserts by others may still occur (phantoms).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Engines use row/version mechanisms, not global SELECT locks.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Indexes are disabled to avoid deadlocks.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only one table may be referenced per transaction.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transaction schedules are equivalent to some serial (one-at-a-time) order.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All queries execute in parallel without any locks.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Serializable is the strongest ANSI level: no anomalies from interleaving.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Indexes remain active.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Multi-table transactions are allowed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Serializable still uses locking or validation.

choices.label: A
choices.body: A stored query definition that behaves like a virtual table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: An index organized by column cardinality.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A transaction isolation level.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A physical copy of data refreshed only on database restart.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Views encapsulate queries; some are updatable under strict rules.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Indexes are storage structures, not view definitions.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Isolation levels are transaction properties.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes a materialized view.

medium.prompt: ON DELETE CASCADE on a foreign key means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Deletes are forbidden on the parent table.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deleting a parent row automatically deletes referencing child rows.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The child table is dropped from the schema.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Child rows become orphaned with NULL primary keys.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: CASCADE propagates deletes (and UPDATE CASCADE propagates key changes) along the FK.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is RESTRICT/NO ACTION, not CASCADE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: CASCADE removes rows, not tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: SET NULL or RESTRICT behave differently; CASCADE removes children.

choices.label: A
choices.body: The number of columns in the SELECT list.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The fraction of rows the predicate is expected to match.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The width of VARCHAR columns in bytes.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The maximum transaction isolation level.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Low selectivity (high match fraction) favors sequential scans; high selectivity favors indexes.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Projection width is unrelated to predicate selectivity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Column width affects I/O size, not match fraction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation is transactional, not selectivity.

choices.label: A
choices.body: The optimizer's chosen plan operators and estimated costs (and actual timings with ANALYZE).

choices.label: B
choices.body: The complete history of every committed transaction.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The ER diagram rendered as SVG.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A list of all user passwords in hashed form.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Plan output reveals joins, scans, index usage, and cost estimates for tuning.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Transaction logs are separate audit/recovery artifacts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: EXPLAIN is execution-plan text, not modeling diagrams.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Security catalogs are not EXPLAIN output.

choices.label: A
choices.body: Transactions always run at SERIALIZABLE.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Foreign-key values reference existing primary-key values (or defined exceptions).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every column has a UNIQUE constraint.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All queries use indexes.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: FK constraints tie child tuples to valid parents unless ON DELETE/UPDATE rules apply.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Default isolation varies by system.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Uniqueness is optional per column.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The optimizer chooses access paths; integrity is constraint-based.

medium.prompt: A materialized view differs from an ordinary view because it…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Cannot be queried with SQL.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Stores the result set physically and must be refreshed to stay current.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Replaces the write-ahead log for durability.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Automatically enforces 5NF on base tables.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Materialized views trade freshness for read performance via stored answers.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Materialized views are queried like tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Durability still uses logging mechanisms.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Normal forms are design properties, not view features.

hard.prompt: Fourth normal form (4NF) addresses…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Lossless join without dependency preservation.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Multivalued dependencies: independent multi-valued facts about the same key should be split.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Transitive dependencies among non-key attributes only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Partial dependencies on part of a composite key.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: 4NF separates unrelated multi-valued sets (e.g., skills and languages for an employee).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That is decomposition theory, not the 4NF definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Transitive dependencies are 3NF concerns.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Partial dependencies are 2NF concerns.

hard.prompt: Fifth normal form (5NF), or PJ/NF, deals with…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Encrypting attributes at rest.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only tables with exactly five columns.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Join dependencies that cannot be reconstructed from smaller projections without spurious tuples.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mandatory clustered indexes on foreign keys.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: 5NF splits relations when join recombination invents extra rows not present in the original.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Security is orthogonal to PJ/NF.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The 'fifth' refers to normal form level, not column count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Physical design is separate from 5NF.

hard.prompt: A nested-loop join is often chosen when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both inputs are huge unsorted heaps with no indexes.

choices.label: B
choices.body: One input is small and indexed lookups on the inner table are cheap per outer row.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The optimizer must guarantee SERIALIZABLE isolation.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All predicates are non-equality cross products.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Nested-loop probes the inner for each outer row; it excels with selective indexes on the inner key.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Large unsorted inputs favor hash or merge joins.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Isolation is independent of join algorithm choice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Cross products are expensive; nested-loop still needs join predicates for equi-joins.

hard.prompt: A hash join typically builds a hash table on…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The smaller (build) input, probing with the larger (probe) input.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always the alphabetically first table name.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The transaction log to ensure durability.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only columns with UNIQUE constraints disabled.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Hash joins partition by join key on the build side, then probe hashes for matches.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Optimizers pick build side by size/cardinality, not name.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Logs are recovery structures, not join hash tables.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Uniqueness affects plan cost but not the build/probe roles directly.

hard.prompt: An index-only scan is possible when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The query performs arbitrary user-defined functions on heap-only columns.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The table has no primary key defined.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The isolation level is READ UNCOMMITTED only.

choices.label: D
choices.body: All required columns appear in the index (including INCLUDE/ covering columns) so heap access is unnecessary.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Visibility map and index tuple versions must allow answering from the index leaf pages alone.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Heap columns force heap fetches unless expressions are indexed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Primary keys are unrelated to index-only feasibility.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Isolation affects visibility, but covering columns are the main requirement.

hard.prompt: A phantom read occurs when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Two transactions deadlock on the same row.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The database returns an error on the first SELECT.

choices.label: C
choices.body: A transaction reads the same row twice with different uncommitted values.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A transaction re-issues a range query and sees new rows committed by another transaction.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Phantoms are new tuples appearing in a range; repeatable read may block some but not all engines block phantoms.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Deadlock is lock cycling, not phantom inserts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Errors are unrelated to phantom anomaly definition.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Uncommitted changes imply dirty/non-repeatable reads, not phantoms.

hard.prompt: Snapshot isolation (common in MVCC engines) provides…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Strict serial equivalence identical to two-phase locking in all cases.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Automatic normalization to BCNF on commit.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Consistent reads of committed data as of a transaction start snapshot, but may allow write skew without extra rules.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Dirty reads of uncommitted transactions.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Readers see a stable snapshot; writers may conflict; write skew needs careful handling beyond SI alone.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Snapshot isolation is not always equivalent to full serializability.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Schema normal forms are design-time, not commit-time.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: MVCC snapshots hide uncommitted writes.

hard.prompt: Two-phase locking (2PL) ensures conflict-serializability by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Never acquiring shared locks on reads.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Growing locks until the transaction reaches its peak, then shrinking locks only after commit/abort begins.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disabling all indexes during updates.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Committing immediately after the first read.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Strict 2PL holds all locks until end of transaction, preventing cascading rollbacks of schedules.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Shared locks are part of 2PL for reads.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Indexes remain; locking governs interleaving.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Early commit would release locks too soon.

hard.prompt: Write skew happens when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The database rejects all SERIALIZABLE transactions.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Two transactions read overlapping data, make disjoint writes based on stale reads, and together violate an invariant.

choices.label: C
choices.body: An index is rebuilt during SELECT.

choices.label: D
choices.body: A single UPDATE touches every row in the table.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Classic example: two doctors on-call checks each read count≥1, both go off-call, leaving zero—needs serializable or constraints.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Serializable prevents write skew; it does not define it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Maintenance operations are unrelated.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bulk update is not write skew.

hard.prompt: Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) typically…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Validates at commit that no conflicting writes occurred since the transaction's snapshot/read set.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Locks every row on first SELECT FOR UPDATE automatically.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Disallows any read operations.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Requires denormalized schemas only.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: OCC assumes low conflict: read freely, check versions/validation on commit, abort if conflict detected.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is pessimistic locking, not OCC.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: OCC relies on reads with validation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Schema style is independent of OCC.

hard.prompt: A partial index (filtered index) indexes…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Only rows that violate foreign keys.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Only temporary tables in the information schema.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only rows satisfying a predicate (e.g., WHERE active = true), reducing size and maintenance cost.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every column in the table including LOB blobs always.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Partial indexes target hot subsets (active users, open orders) for selective queries.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Invalid rows should not exist if constraints enforce integrity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Partial indexes apply to user tables with predicates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Partial means row filter, not all columns by default.

hard.prompt: A decomposition is lossless when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: All functional dependencies are eliminated entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Every attribute appears in only one relation regardless of dependencies.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The database removes all foreign keys.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Joining the projected relations recovers exactly the original tuples without spurious rows.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Lossless join tests (e.g., chase) ensure natural join of fragments equals the source relation.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Dependencies should be preserved when possible.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Dependency preservation is a separate goal.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Foreign keys express relationships; lossless join is relational algebra property.

hard.prompt: BCNF can be stricter than 3NF when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: A relation has overlapping candidate keys so a non-superkey determinant remains.

choices.label: B
choices.body: All attributes are prime (part of some candidate key).

choices.label: C
choices.body: The table has no functional dependencies at all.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Every determinant is a single-attribute primary key.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Classic example: R(Student, Course, Instructor) with Instructor → Course is in 3NF but not BCNF if (Student, Course) is key.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That is 3NF-by-definition case where BCNF may still differ with overlapping keys.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Without FDs, normal forms trivially hold.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Then BCNF and 3NF often coincide.

hard.prompt: Histogram statistics in the catalog help the optimizer…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Guarantee zero deadlocks globally.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Estimate predicate selectivity and data distribution per column.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Store undo logs for every SELECT query.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Encrypt data at rest with AES-256 automatically.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Histograms capture non-uniform distributions better than single average row width alone.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Deadlocks can still occur with accurate stats.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SELECT does not generate undo; DML does.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Encryption is security configuration.

hard.prompt: A cost-based optimizer chooses plans by…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Ignoring table statistics entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Estimating resource costs (I/O, CPU, memory) for alternative physical operators and picking a low-cost plan.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Executing every possible plan fully before choosing.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always picking nested-loop joins regardless of size.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: CBO uses stats (row counts, NDV, histograms) and cost models to compare join orders and access paths.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Stats are central to cost estimation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That would be prohibitively expensive; estimates suffice.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: CBO weighs hash/merge/nested-loop based on estimates.

hard.prompt: Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 2 tracking typically…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Stores a new row with new surrogate key and effective dates when an attribute changes, preserving history.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Deletes the dimension table on each change.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Stores only the current value in a flat file outside the database.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Overwrites the old row in place without history.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Type 2 adds version rows (valid_from/valid_to, is_current) for warehouse history.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Dimensions persist; versions accumulate.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SCD Type 2 is a relational warehousing pattern.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That is Type 1 overwrite.

hard.prompt: OLTP schemas differ from OLAP star schemas mainly because OLTP…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Normalizes data to support many small concurrent writes with integrity constraints.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Disallows transactions and indexes.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Requires every query to scan all partitions fully.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Stores only denormalized fact tables without dimensions.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: OLTP favors normalized operational tables; OLAP favors denormalized stars for analytic scans.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: OLTP relies heavily on transactions and indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Analytic scans are OLAP; OLTP targets point lookups/short updates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Star schemas with facts and dimensions are OLAP.

hard.prompt: Choosing a natural key over a surrogate key is preferable when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Surrogate keys are prohibited by SQL standards.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The business identifier is stable, unique, and small enough for efficient joins.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The identifier frequently changes format or merges across legacy systems.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Composite keys always slow every join and must be avoided even if stable.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Natural keys (ISBN, country code) expose meaning; surrogates help when natural keys change or are wide.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: SQL allows both; choice is engineering tradeoff.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Instability favors surrogates.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Stable composite natural keys are valid when modeled carefully.

hard.prompt: For composite index (a, b, c), a query filtering on b and c alone without a predicate on a…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Always performs an index-only scan on all three leading columns.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Forces the database to drop the primary key.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Often cannot use the index for a pure index range scan on b,c due to left-prefix rules (unless index skip scan exists).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Requires SERIALIZABLE isolation to read any rows.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: B-tree composite indexes are ordered by leading columns; skipping 'a' breaks contiguous range access.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Missing leading column usually blocks efficient range use.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Primary keys are independent of secondary index prefix rules.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Isolation does not govern index prefix usability.

hard.prompt: Index merge (intersection/union) plans combine…

choices.label: A
choices.body: User passwords with hash join build sides.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Multiple single-column (or narrow) indexes to satisfy AND/OR predicates when one composite index is unavailable.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Only full-table scans because indexes cannot be combined.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Two unrelated databases on different hosts without federation.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Optimizers may bitmap-or/and rowid sets from several indexes to filter rows before heap access.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Security data is unrelated to index intersection plans.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Index merge exists precisely to combine indexes.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Index merge is intra-database plan choice.
